carFuel.explanation: Each car’s monthly fuel cost is distance ÷ mileage × fuel price, plus any extra upkeep. The CNG car’s saving adds up month by month, and it breaks even when that running total covers the extra price of the CNG variant. The stricter test also charges interest on the extra price, at your loan rate or what the money could have earned, compounded monthly. Fuel prices rise each year by the rates you set; by default they stay flat.

carFuel.faq.1.q: Why are there two break-even figures?
carFuel.faq.1.a: Without interest, break-even is when the fuel saved equals the extra price. With interest, the extra price also grows at your loan rate, because that money was borrowed or could have earned elsewhere. The second figure comes later, and the verdict uses it.
carFuel.faq.2.q: Where do the fuel prices come from?
carFuel.faq.2.a: Choose your city under Assumptions. Verified city prices fill in automatically, with their source and date in the table above. Prices change daily, so check your local pump.
carFuel.faq.3.q: Does it include resale value, insurance or kit servicing?
carFuel.faq.3.a: Resale value and insurance are not included. Add any extra yearly running cost, such as cylinder testing or kit servicing, under Extra upkeep.
carFuel.faq.4.q: What if I drive less than the example?
carFuel.faq.4.a: The saving shrinks with distance. “What would flip the answer” shows the monthly distance below which petrol wins with your numbers.

solar.metaDescription: Rooftop solar payback with your own bill: payback year, savings over 25 years and yearly return, with every assumption shown.
solar.explanation: Each month, the panels generate system size × generation per kW per day × 365 ÷ 12 units, less a little each year as they age. Your bill is worked out twice: on all the units you use, and on only the units you still buy from the grid, minus credit for any units you send to it. The difference is the saving. Because the bill uses the tariff's slabs, the units you save come off the most expensive slab first. Payback is the month when savings cover the price after subsidy.
solar.faq.1.a: Subsidy, generation, panel loss and export credit depend on rules and data we have not verified yet, so we do not guess them. Enter the figures from your installer's quote and your bill.
solar.faq.2.q: Why do I enter an average price per unit?
solar.faq.2.a: Until the UP slab tariff is verified, the tool uses one price for every unit plus your fixed charge. Divide your energy charge and duty by the units on your bill to get it.
solar.faq.3.a: The interest rate at which the money you put into the system would grow to the same savings. Compare it with what the money would earn elsewhere, after tax.

rentBuy.metaDescription: Rent or buy a home, with your own numbers: net worth of each path after the years you choose, when buying overtakes renting, and the home price growth it needs.
rentBuy.explanation: The tool follows two households month by month. The buyer pays the EMI, maintenance and property tax. The renter pays rent and invests what the buyer spent at purchase. Each month, whoever pays less invests the difference at your return. At the end, the buyer's net worth is the home's value less the loan still owed and the cost of selling, plus anything they invested; the renter's is their investments plus the deposit back.
rentBuy.faq.1.a: Because the renter invests the down payment and stamp duty instead of spending them, and keeps investing whenever rent is cheaper than owning. If your return beats home price growth after costs, renting and investing can end ahead.
rentBuy.faq.2.a: Not yet. They depend on your tax regime and the current rules, which we have not verified. Leaving them out makes buying look slightly worse than it may be under the old regime.
rentBuy.faq.3.a: What the renter's money would actually earn after tax, in whatever they would really invest it in. A lower figure favours buying; a higher one favours renting.

page.methodology.title: How we work out the numbers
page.methodology.description: The formulas behind every Decidewise calculator, in plain language: monthly simulation, EMI, break-even, scenarios, what flips the answer, and today's rupees.
page.methodology.intro: Every tool runs the same way: a month-by-month simulation of each option, using only the figures you can see and change on the page. This page sets out the rules they share and the formula behind each tool. The code that does the maths is tested against numbers worked out by hand.
page.methodology.conventions.title: Rules every tool follows
page.methodology.conventions.body:
Time moves in months. A tool starts at month 0, the day you decide, and steps forward one month at a time to the end of the period you choose.

Prices that rise each year (fuel, electricity, rent) stay flat for twelve months and then step up by the yearly rate. Investment returns and home prices grow a little every month, at the monthly rate that adds up to the yearly figure you enter.

Nothing is rounded until it is displayed.
page.methodology.conventions.formula:
monthly rate     = (1 + yearly rate)^(1/12) − 1
price in year y  = starting price × (1 + yearly rise)^(y − 1)
page.methodology.loan.title: Loans and EMI
page.methodology.loan.body: Loan rates are quoted the way banks quote them: a yearly rate divided by 12 for each month. The EMI is the fixed monthly payment that clears the loan exactly at the end of the tenure. Each month, interest is charged on what is still owed and the rest of the EMI repays the loan.
page.methodology.loan.formula:
r   = yearly rate ÷ 12
n   = tenure in months
EMI = loan × r × (1 + r)^n ÷ ((1 + r)^n − 1)
page.methodology.breakeven.title: Break-even
page.methodology.breakeven.body: Break-even is the first month in which the running total of what an option saves catches up with what it cost upfront. If that never happens within the period you chose, the tool says so instead of guessing beyond it.
page.methodology.scenarios.title: Scenarios and what flips the answer
page.methodology.scenarios.body:
The pessimistic, base and optimistic results rerun the same calculation with the values in the default scenario table, changing only the inputs the table covers. They are a range of reasonable assumptions, not forecasts.

"What would flip the answer" changes one input at a time and holds everything else. It searches for the value at which the result crosses zero, which is where the other option starts to win.
page.methodology.todaysRupees.title: Today's rupees
page.methodology.todaysRupees.body: A lakh in fifteen years buys less than a lakh today. Where a tool shows an amount in today's rupees, it divides the future amount by inflation over the same period.
page.methodology.carFuel.title: Petrol, CNG or EV
page.methodology.carFuel.body:
For each car, the monthly running cost is the fuel or electricity for your distance plus a twelfth of the yearly upkeep. The saving is the petrol car's cost minus the other car's.

The extra purchase price is charged interest at the rate you enter, because that money is either borrowed or not invested. Break-even is the month the running total of savings reaches the extra price with interest added. The savings themselves are not assumed to be invested.

For an EV, the price per unit blends home and public charging by the share you charge at home.
page.methodology.carFuel.formula:
monthly cost   = km a month ÷ mileage × fuel price + yearly upkeep ÷ 12
extra price(m) = extra price × (1 + rate ÷ 12)^m
EV unit price  = home share × home rate + (1 − home share) × public rate
page.methodology.solar.title: Rooftop solar
page.methodology.solar.body:
Each month, the tool works out your electricity bill twice through the state's slab tariff: once for your full use, and once for what is left after solar. Because the bill is worked out slab by slab, the units solar saves come off the most expensive slab first.

Units you export beyond your own use earn the export rate. The bill with solar never drops below the fixed charges. Panel output falls each year by the degradation rate, and the tariff rises once a year.

Payback is the first month the savings add up to the system's cost after subsidy. The return (IRR) is the yearly rate at which those savings exactly repay that cost.
page.methodology.solar.formula:
generation = kW × units per kW per day × 365 ÷ 12 × (1 − degradation)^(year − 1)
saving     = bill without solar − bill with solar
IRR        = (1 + monthly IRR)^12 − 1
page.methodology.rentBuy.title: Rent or buy
page.methodology.rentBuy.body:
The tool follows two households. The buyer pays the down payment, stamp duty and other purchase costs, then each month the EMI, maintenance on the home's value, and property tax that rises with inflation. The renter pays rent that rises once a year, and invests what the buyer spent at purchase, less the security deposit.

Each month, whoever pays less invests the difference at your return. At the end, each side's net worth is compared.
page.methodology.rentBuy.formula:
buyer net worth  = home value − loan still owed − cost of selling + buyer's investments
renter net worth = renter's investments + security deposit
page.methodology.limits.title: What the tools leave out
page.methodology.limits.body: Each tool lists the money factors it does not model, and a checklist of the things that are not about money. Where a value is not verified yet, the tool says so and asks you for your own figure instead of filling one in.

page.about.title: About Decidewise
page.about.description: Why Decidewise exists, who it is for, and how it is built.
page.about.intro: Decidewise is a set of calculators for big money decisions in India: the kind that cost a lakh or more and that people usually make on a salesperson's numbers.
page.about.why.title: Why it exists
page.about.why.body: Most calculators show one confident answer and hide the assumptions behind it. A small change in fuel prices, rent or your return can flip that answer. Decidewise shows every assumption, lets you change it, and tells you what would have to change for the other option to win.
page.about.how.title: How it works
page.about.how.body: Every tool runs in your browser. Nothing you type is sent anywhere. The formulas are set out on the methodology page and checked against figures worked out by hand. Prices, rates and rules come from the sources listed on each tool and in the assumptions changelog.
page.about.author.title: Who makes it
page.about.contact.title: Found a mistake?
page.about.contact.body: Use the "Report an error" link at the bottom of any tool. Say which number looks wrong and why, and include a source if you have one.
page.disclaimer.title: Disclaimer
page.disclaimer.description: Decidewise is for education only. It is not investment, tax or insurance advice.
page.disclaimer.intro: Decidewise helps you think through a decision with your own numbers. It does not tell you what to do.
page.disclaimer.education.title: Education, not advice
page.disclaimer.education.body: Nothing on this site is investment, tax, legal or insurance advice. Decidewise is not registered with SEBI as an investment adviser or research analyst, and is not registered with IRDAI. Speak to a qualified, registered professional before you act on a large decision.
page.disclaimer.estimates.title: Results are estimates
page.disclaimer.estimates.body: Every result depends on the assumptions shown next to it. Prices, rates, tariffs, subsidies and tax rules change, and the values here may be out of date by the time you read them. Returns, price rises and growth rates are assumptions you can edit, not predictions.
page.disclaimer.products.title: No product recommendations
page.disclaimer.products.body: Decidewise does not recommend any product, fund, scheme, lender, insurer, car or installer.
page.disclaimer.check.title: Check before you act
page.disclaimer.check.body: Confirm prices, rates and rules with the seller, bank or authority concerned before you decide. If you find a mistake, please report it so it can be fixed for everyone.

page.privacy.title: Privacy
page.privacy.description: Decidewise collects no personal data. The calculators run in your browser and store your settings only on your device.
page.privacy.intro: Decidewise has no accounts and no sign-up, and the calculators send nothing you type to any server.
page.privacy.device.title: What stays on your device
page.privacy.device.body: The figures you set in the Assumptions panel and your light or dark theme choice are saved in your browser's local storage, so they are there next time. Whether the logo animation has played is kept for the current visit only. None of this leaves your device. Use "Reset all" in the Assumptions panel, or clear this site's data in your browser, to remove it.
page.privacy.cookies.title: Cookies
page.privacy.links.title: Share links
page.privacy.links.body: When you copy a link to a result, the inputs are written into the link itself. Anyone you send it to can see them. Links contain only numbers and options, never names or contact details.
page.privacy.analytics.title: Analytics
page.privacy.analytics.body: Decidewise does not use analytics or advertising trackers today. If analytics are added, they will be a privacy-friendly service that sets no cookies, and this page will name it before it is switched on.
page.privacy.thirdParty.title: Other services
page.privacy.thirdParty.body:
Fonts and scripts are served from this site, not from third parties. The host that serves the site may keep standard technical logs, such as the pages requested and IP addresses, to run and protect it.

If you report an error, your email app sends the message, and we receive your email address with it. It is used only to reply.

page.trademarks.identification.body: Names are used only to identify a product, fuel or source. Using a name does not mean that its owner endorses Decidewise, or that Decidewise endorses the product.
page.trademarks.affiliation.title: No affiliation
page.trademarks.affiliation.body: Decidewise is independent. It is not affiliated with, sponsored by or paid by any manufacturer, lender, insurer, fuel company, electricity distributor or government body named on the site.
page.trademarks.logos.title: No logos or manufacturer images
page.trademarks.logos.body: Decidewise does not use logos or manufacturer images. If you own a name used here and think it is used wrongly, please contact us through the "Report an error" link on any tool.
page.notFound.title: Page not found
page.notFound.body: The link may be old or mistyped. These are the calculators that exist today:
inputs.quickLegend: Start with the few things only you know. Everything else is filled in under “Refine the assumptions”; fields marked “Check this” are worth a look.
refine.title: Refine the assumptions
carFuel.refineHint: Fuel prices, mileage, interest, years, price rises, upkeep, insurance, resale and one-off costs. Already filled in.
carFuel.needPricesAll: Enter the on-road price of all three cars to see which costs least.
note.insurance: Yearly premium. Optional: leave empty if it is about the same for each car.
note.resale: What it sells for after {years} years, as a share of the on-road price. Your estimate; optional.
note.cngOneOff: A big one-time cost, such as replacing the cylinder. Optional.
note.evOneOff: A big one-time cost, such as a battery replacement outside warranty. Optional.
note.oneOffYear: The year the one-off cost falls in.
verdict.resaleDetail: {winner} does not earn back its extra price on running costs alone; its higher resale value puts it ahead at the end.
stat.netHelpResale: Running costs saved minus the extra price and its interest, plus the difference in resale at the end.
carSet.headline: Over {years} years, {car} costs least
carSet.gaps: {second} costs {gap2} more and {third} {gap3} more, counting the price, interest, running costs and resale.
carSet.caption: Total cost of owning each car over {years} years
carSet.row.running: Fuel, upkeep and other costs, {years} years
carSet.help: Interest is charged on each car's full price, at the rate you entered, because that money is borrowed or not invested.
chart.setTitle: Each car against petrol, over time
scenarios.heading: Saved scenarios
scenarios.name: Scenario {n}
scenarios.limit: You can keep up to {n}. Remove one to save another.
rentBuy.group.essentials: The home, the rent and your money
rentBuy.refineHint: Down payment, other costs, loan tenure, prepayment, income, property tax, deposit, home price growth, rent increase and inflation. Already filled in or optional.
rentBuy.in.prepayYearly: Extra paid on the loan each year
rentBuy.note.prepayYearly: Paid after the twelfth EMI each year; the EMI stays the same, so the loan ends sooner. Optional.
rentBuy.note.monthlyIncome: Optional. Only used to show what share of it the EMI takes.
rentBuy.stat.emiShare: EMI as a share of income
solar.refineHint: Fixed charge, export credit, panel ageing, tariff rise, years and inverter replacement. Filled in or optional.
solar.stat.coverage: Share of your use covered, year 1
